title: The Competition (Amendment) Bill, 2022
input:
Highlights of the Bill
The Bill seeks to amend the Competition Act, 2002, to regulate mergers and acquisitions based on the value of transactions.  Deals with transaction value of more than Rs 2,000 crore will require CCI’s approval.  The Bill proposes to reduce the timeline for the CCI to pass an order on such transactions from 210 days to 150 days.
The Bill expands the scope of entities that can be adjudged to be a part of anti-competitive agreements.  Currently, enterprises or persons engaged in similar businesses can be held to be a part of anti-competitive agreements.  The Bill expands this to also include enterprises or persons who are not engaged in similar businesses.
The Bill provides a framework for settlement and commitment for faster resolution of investigations of anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position.
The Bill decriminalises certain offences under the Act by changing the nature of punishment from imposition of fine to civil penalties.  These offences include failure to comply with orders of the CCI and directions of the Director General related to anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position.
Key Issues and Analysis
Acquisitions in the digital markets are valued based on data or certain business innovation of the company being acquired.  Acquisition of such entities may not fall under the purview of traditional thresholds of assets or turnover to evaluate their impact on competition.  The Bill proposes to evaluate such deals based on the value of transactions.
The Bill expands the powers of the Director General for investigating contraventions under the Act.  This includes the power to seek information and documents from legal advisers also.  This may be at variance with the provisions of lawyer-client confidentiality under section 126 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
The Bill mandates depositing 25% of any amount levied by CCI prior to filing an appeal against a CCI order before the NCLAT.  The question is whether specifying a mandatory deposit in the law is appropriate.
The Act allows the use of intellectual property rights as a defence in cases of anti-competitive agreements.  This defence is not available in cases involving abuse of dominant position.  The Bill does not address this gap.
PART A: HIGHLIGHTS OF THE BILL
Context
The Competition Act, 2002 was enacted to promote and sustain competition in markets, protect the interest of consumers, and ensure freedom of trade for market participants.
[1]
It established the Competition Commission of India (CCI) to eliminate practices having adverse effect on market competition.  Under the Act, enterprises are not allowed to enter into anti-competitive agreements which can cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition in India or abuse their dominant position.  Persons and enterprises are also not allowed to enter into a combination which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within the relevant market in India.  Combinations are defined as the acquisition, merger or amalgamation of one or more enterprises.  Combinations that meet certain thresholds based on their assets or turnover have to be notified for CCI’s approval.
Since the Competition Act came into force, Indian markets have grown significantly.
[2]
There has also been changes in the way businesses operate with the emergence of digital internet based companies and new age markets involving technology.
2
In 2018, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs constituted the Competition Law Review Committee to ensure that the Competition Act is in line with India’s economic fundamentals.
[3]
In its deliberations, the Committee noted that certain market practices are not adequately covered by the current regulatory framework.
2
The Committee released its report in 2019 and suggested several amendments to the Act and changes in the regulatory structure dealing with matters of market competition.  The Competition (Amendment) Bill, 2022, was introduced after reviewing the recommendations proposed by the Competition Law Review Committee.  The Bill seeks to broaden the scope of anti-competitive agreements, provide for evaluation of combinations based on value of transactions, reduce the time limit for approval of combinations, and introduce settlement and commitment framework to reduce litigation.
Key Features
Regulation of combinations based on transaction value:
The Act prohibits any person or enterprise from entering into a combination which may cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition.  Combinations imply mergers, acquisitions, or amalgamation of enterprises. The prohibition applies to transactions where parties involved have: (i) cumulative assets of more than Rs 1,000 crore, or (ii) cumulative turnover of more than Rs 3,000 crore, subject to certain other conditions. The Bill expands the definition of combinations to include transactions with a value above Rs 2,000 crore.

**Competition (Amendment) Bill, 2022 – Plain‑English Summary**

---

### 1. Why the Bill Was Introduced  
- **Original law:** The Competition Act 2002 created the Competition Commission of India (CCI) to stop anti‑competitive behaviour and protect consumers.  
- **Changes in the market:** Since 2002, Indian markets have grown and digital/technology‑driven businesses have become common.  
- **Review:** In 2018 the Ministry of Corporate Affairs set up a Competition Law Review Committee. Its 2019 report recommended several updates to the Act.  
- **Result:** The Competition (Amendment) Bill 2022 incorporates many of those recommendations.

---

### 2. Main Changes Proposed by the Bill  

#### a. Regulation of Mergers & Acquisitions (called “combinations”)  
- **New threshold:** Any merger, acquisition, or amalgamation with a **transaction value above Rs 2,000 crore** must be approved by the CCI.  
- **Current thresholds:** Previously, approval was required only when the combined assets were > Rs 1,000 crore **or** turnover was > Rs 3,000 crore.  
- **Purpose:** Allows the CCI to look at big deals that are valued mainly on data or innovation (common in digital markets), not just on assets or turnover.

#### b. Faster approval process  
- **Time limit cut:** The period for the CCI to give a decision on such high‑value transactions is reduced from **210 days to 150 days**.

#### c. Broader definition of anti‑competitive agreements  
- **Now includes:** Companies or persons **not in the same line of business** can be found guilty of anti‑competitive agreements.  
- **Before:** Only firms doing similar business could be held liable.

#### d. Settlement and commitment mechanism  
- **New framework:** Parties can settle investigations or give commitments to the CCI, speeding up resolution and reducing court cases.

#### e. De‑criminalisation of certain offences  
- **Switch to civil penalties:** Offences such as **failure to obey CCI orders or Director‑General directions** will no longer attract criminal fines; they will be treated as civil penalties (financial fines).

---

### 3. Additional Issues Highlighted in the Bill  

- **Digital‑market deals:** Because many tech companies are valued on data or innovation rather than assets, the value‑based threshold helps capture those transactions.  
- **Director‑General’s investigative powers:** The Bill lets the Director‑General request information **including from a company’s legal advisers**. This could clash with lawyer‑client confidentiality under Section 126 of the Indian Evidence Act 1872.  
- **Mandatory deposit for appeals:** Before appealing a CCI order to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), a party must deposit **25 % of any CCI‑imposed amount**. The Bill does not explain whether a compulsory deposit is appropriate.  
- **Intellectual‑property defence gap:** The current Act allows a defence based on IP rights for anti‑competitive agreements, but **not** for abuse of dominant position. The Bill does not close this gap.

---

### 4. Timeline & Jurisdiction  

| Year | Event |
|------|-------|
| **2002** | Competition Act enacted; CCI created. |
| **2018** | Competition Law Review Committee formed. |
| **2019** | Committee’s report released with amendment suggestions. |
| **2022** | Competition (Amendment) Bill introduced in Parliament. |
| **India** | All provisions apply nationwide; CCI and NCLAT are the key authorities. |

---

### 5. What This Means for Businesses  

- **Large deals (> Rs 2,000 crore)** must be cleared by the CCI before they close.  
- **Approval will be faster** (max 150 days).  
- Companies can be penalised for anti‑competitive conduct **even if they operate in different sectors**.  
- **Settlements** are now an option, potentially avoiding lengthy litigation.  
- Certain violations will be treated as **civil fines**, not criminal offences.  
- Firms must be ready to **provide documents from legal counsel** if asked, and to **pay a 25 % deposit** before appealing CCI decisions.  

---

title: The Bharatiya Sakshya Bill, 2023

Highlights of the Bill
The Bharatiya Sakshya Bill, 2023 (BSB) replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (IEA).  It retains most provisions of the IEA including those on confessions, relevancy of facts, and burden of proof.
The IEA provides for two kinds of evidence - documentary and oral.  Documentary evidence includes primary (original documents) and secondary (that proves the contents of the original).  The BSB retains the distinction.  It includes electronic records in the definition of documents.
Under the IEA, electronic records are categorised as secondary evidence.  The BSB classifies electronic records as primary evidence.  It expands such records to include information stored in semiconductor memory or any communication devices (smartphones, laptops).
Under the IEA, secondary evidence may be required under various conditions, such as when the original is in the possession of the person against whom the document is sought to be proved or has been destroyed.  The BSB adds that secondary evidence may be required if the genuineness of the document itself is in question.
Key Issues and Analysis
The Supreme Court has recognised that electronic records may be tampered with.  While the BSB provides for the admissibility of such records, there are no safeguards to prevent the tampering and contamination of such records during the investigation process.
Currently, electronic records must be authenticated by a certificate to be admissible as documents.  The BSB retains these provisions for admissibility.  The BSB also classifies electronic evidence as documents (which may not need certification).  This creates a contradiction.
Under the IEA, a fact discovered due to information received from an accused in police custody may be provable.  The BSB retains this provision.   Courts and Committees noted that facts may be discovered in police custody by coercion, and without adequate safeguards.
The IEA (and the BSB) allows such information to be admissible if it was obtained when the accused was in police custody, but not if he was outside.  The Law Commission recommended to remove this distinction.
The Law Commission has made several recommendations, which have not been incorporated.  These include the presumption that the police officer caused the injuries if an accused was injured in police custody.

**Bharatiya Sakshya Bill, 2023 – Plain‑English Summary**

---

### 1. What the Bill Does
- Replaces the **Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (IEA)**.
- Keeps most of the IEA’s rules (confessions, relevance of facts, burden of proof, etc.).
- Applies to **all civil and criminal cases** in India.

---

### 2. Types of Evidence

| Category | IEA definition | BSB change |
|----------|----------------|------------|
| **Documentary evidence** | Written papers, maps, drawings. Divided into **primary** (original) and **secondary** (copies or proof of the original). | Adds **electronic records** (emails, texts, data on smartphones, laptops, semiconductor memory, etc.) as **documents**. Treats electronic records as **primary evidence** instead of secondary. |
| **Oral evidence** | Testimony spoken in court. | No change. |

---

### 3. Primary vs. Secondary Evidence

- **Primary evidence** – the original document or the original electronic file.
- **Secondary evidence** – a copy, a certified copy, or any proof of the contents when the original is unavailable **or** when the document’s authenticity is in doubt (new BSB rule).

---

### 4. Confessions and Police Custody

- **Confessions to police officers** – **inadmissible**.
- **Confessions made while in police custody** – inadmissible **unless** recorded by a Magistrate.
- **Information obtained from an accused in custody** – can be used **only** if it directly leads to a discovered fact.
- The **Law Commission** has suggested removing the “in‑custody only” rule, but the Bill has not adopted this change.

---

### 5. Electronic Evidence – Issues Highlighted

- Courts recognize that electronic records can be **tampered with**.
- The Bill allows such records but **does not add new safeguards** against tampering during investigations.
- Current rule: electronic records must be **authenticated by a certificate** to be admissible.  
  - The Bill also calls electronic evidence a “document,” which sometimes **does not require certification**, creating a contradiction.

---

### 6. Law Commission Recommendations Not Adopted

- **Presumption of police‑caused injury** if an accused is injured while in custody.  
- Other suggestions on custodial violence, police confessions, and cross‑examination remain **unincorporated**.

---

### 7. Historical Context (Key Amendments to the IEA)

| Year | Amendment | What Changed |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| **2000** | Electronic records allowed as **secondary** evidence. | First recognition of digital documents. |
| **2013** | Added rules on **consent in rape cases**. | Shifted burden to the accused to prove consent; victim’s character and sexual history made irrelevant. |

---

### 8. Legislative Journey

- **Introduced in Lok Sabha:** **11 August 2023**.
- **Reviewed by:** Standing Committee on Home Affairs.
- **Status:** Pending final parliamentary approval.

---

### 9. Key Take‑aways

- The Bill **modernises** evidence law by treating electronic data as original documents.
- It **keeps** most of the old IEA rules, especially on relevance, burden of proof, and inadmissibility of police confessions.
- **Concerns** remain about the security of electronic evidence and the lack of new safeguards.
- Several **Law Commission** suggestions aimed at protecting accused persons in custody have **not** been included.

title: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Bill, 2026
input:
The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Bill, 2026 was introduced in Rajya Sabha on March 25, 2026.  The Bill seeks to regulate certain matters related to officers of the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs).  Currently, such matters are regulated under respective Acts.  The Bill aims to ensure legislative clarity, preserve operational distinctiveness, and harmonise judicial directions with administrative and federal requirements.
Powers to make Rules:
The Bill empowers the central government to make Rules on matters related to officers of specified CAPFs.  These include recruitment, deputation, promotion, and conditions of service.  The Bill applies to five CAPFs listed in the Schedule to the Bill.  These are:  (i) Central Reserve Police Force, (ii) Border Security Force, (iii) Central Industrial Security Force, (iv) Indo-Tibetan Border Police, and (v) Sashastra Seema Bal.  The central government may amend the Schedule by notification to make the Bill applicable to other CAPFs.  Officers include: (i) Group A (general duty or executive) officers of the rank of Assistant Commandant and above in CAPFs, (ii) officers on deputation from the Indian Police Service (IPS), and (iii) officers of the Indian Army on deputation or re-employment.
The Bill provides that the central government may frame Rules notwithstanding any other law, any judgement or order of any Court, or any government order.  Specified Rules under the respective Acts will continue to apply until amended or replaced.  Any orders on financial benefits will also continue to apply, until new orders are issued.
Positions to be filled by deputation:
The following positions in CAPFs must be filled by deputation of IPS officers:  (i) 50% of the posts in the rank of Inspector General, (ii) a minimum of 67% of the posts in the rank of Additional Director General, and (iii) all posts in the ranks of Director General and Special Director General.
Overriding effect:
In case of any inconsistency between the Bill and any other law, the provisions of the Bill will prevail.

## Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Bill, 2026  

### Introduction  
* Introduced in Rajya Sabha on **March 25 2026**.  
* Intended to regulate matters concerning officers of the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs).  
* Seeks legislative clarity, operational distinctiveness, and alignment of judicial directions with administrative and federal needs.  

### Applicability  
* Covers five CAPFs listed in the Schedule:  
  - Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)  
  - Border Security Force (BSF)  
  - Central Industrial Security Force (CISF)  
  - Indo‑Tibetan Border Police (ITBP)  
  - Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB)  
* The central government can add other CAPFs by issuing a notification.  

### Officers Covered  
* Group A (general duty or executive) officers of rank **Assistant Commandant** and above in the listed CAPFs.  
* Officers on deputation from the **Indian Police Service (IPS)**.  
* Officers of the **Indian Army** on deputation or re‑employment.  

### Powers to Make Rules  
* The central government may make Rules on:  
  - Recruitment  
  - Deputation  
  - Promotion  
  - Conditions of service  
* These Rules can be issued **regardless of any other law, court judgment, or government order**.  
* Existing Rules under the respective Acts remain in force until they are amended or replaced.  
* Current orders on financial benefits continue until new orders are issued.  

### Deputation Requirements for IPS Officers  
* **Inspector General** rank: at least **50 %** of posts must be filled by IPS officers on deputation.  
* **Additional Director General** rank: at least **67 %** of posts must be filled by IPS officers on deputation.  
* **Director General** and **Special Director General** ranks: **all** posts must be filled by IPS officers on deputation.  

### Overriding Effect  
* If any provision of this Bill conflicts with another law, the Bill’s provisions **prevail**.
